claim: Ecological conditions are known to change the expression of mutualisms.
source: Ecological conditions are known to change the expression of mutualisms though the causal agents driving such changes remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field, presented as established knowledge without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: The causal agents driving changes in mutualism expression remain poorly understood.
source: Ecological conditions are known to change the expression of mutualisms though the causal agents driving such changes remain poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Temperature stress modulates the harm threatened by a common enemy.
source: Here we show that temperature stress modulates the harm threatened by a common enemy, and thereby induces a phoretic mite to become a protective mutualist.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Temperature stress induces a phoretic mite to become a protective mutualist.
source: Here we show that temperature stress modulates the harm threatened by a common enemy, and thereby induces a phoretic mite to become a protective mutualist.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mites compete with beetle larvae for food in the absence of blowflies.
source: We show that mites compete with beetle larvae for food in the absence of blowflies, and reduce beetle reproductive success.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Laboratory Experiment 1.

claim: Mites reduce beetle reproductive success in the absence of blowflies.
source: We show that mites compete with beetle larvae for food in the absence of blowflies, and reduce beetle reproductive success.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Laboratory Experiment 1.

claim: When blowflies breed on the carrion, mites enhance beetle reproductive success by eating blowfly eggs.
source: However, when blowflies breed on the carrion too, mites enhance beetle reproductive success by eating blowfly eggs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from field and laboratory experiments.

claim: High densities of mites are especially effective at promoting beetle reproductive success at higher and lower natural ranges in temperature.
source: High densities of mites are especially effective at promoting beetle reproductive success at higher and lower natural ranges in temperature, when blowfly larvae are more potent rivals for the limited resources on the carcass.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from field and laboratory experiments.

claim: Blowfly larvae are more potent rivals for limited resources on the carcass at higher and lower temperatures.
source: High densities of mites are especially effective at promoting beetle reproductive success at higher and lower natural ranges in temperature, when blowfly larvae are more potent rivals for the limited resources on the carcass.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing blowfly reproductive success patterns.

claim: Protective mutualisms among macro-organisms are widespread and well-known.
source: Protective mutualisms among macro-organisms are both widespread and well-known (Clay, 2014; Palmer et al., 2015; Hopkins et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Protective mutualisms involve one species defending another species from attack by a third party species, in exchange for some form of reward.
source: They involve one species defending another species from attack by a third party species, in exchange for some form of reward (Clay, 2014; Palmer et al., 2015; Hopkins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutualisms can evolve when a commensal or mildly parasitic species is induced to become a protective mutualist upon exposure to an environmental stressor.
source: Theoretical analyses predict that mutualisms like this can evolve when a commensal or mildly parasitic species, that lives in or upon its host, is induced to become a protective mutualist upon exposure to an environmental stressor (Fellous and Salvaudon, 2009; Lively et al., 2005; Hopkins et al., 2017; Rafaluk-Mohr et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical analyses.

claim: The environmental stressor that induces mutualism can be biotic.
source: The stressor can be biotic (Ashby and King, 2017; Clay, 2014; Ewald, 1987; Lively et al., 2005; Schwarz and Müller, 1992) or abiotic (Corbin et al., 2017; Engl et al., 2018; Hoang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The environmental stressor that induces mutualism can be abiotic.
source: The stressor can be biotic (Ashby and King, 2017; Clay, 2014; Ewald, 1987; Lively et al., 2005; Schwarz and Müller, 1992) or abiotic (Corbin et al., 2017; Engl et al., 2018; Hoang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The contextual factors that drive variation in the expression of mutualisms on an ecological timescale are relatively less well understood.
source: Although the adaptive evolution of mutualisms has been studied in detail, the contextual factors that drive equivalent variation in the expression of mutualisms on an ecological timescale are relatively less well understood (Chamberlain et al., 2014; Jaenike et al., 2010; Hoeksema and Bruna, 2015), especially for protective mutualisms (Hopkins et al., 2017; Palmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement about the state of the field is supported by citations.

claim: It is unclear how different biotic and abiotic factors combine to influence the expression of a mutualism when conditions vary locally.
source: In particular, it is unclear how different biotic and abiotic factors combine to influence the expression of a mutualism, especially when conditions vary locally.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It is not well understood whether the extent of mutualism is density-dependent.
source: Nor is it well understood whether the extent of mutualism is density-dependent (Hoeksema and Bruna, 2015; Palmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Burying beetles use the dead body of a small vertebrate to breed upon.
source: Our experiments focus on burying beetles (Nicrophorus vespilloides), which use the dead body of a small vertebrate to breed upon (Scott, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about burying beetle biology, supported by citation.

claim: A pair of beetles works together to convert the carcass into an edible carrion nest for their larvae by removing any fur or feathers, and rolling the meat into a ball.
source: A pair of beetles works together to convert the carcass into an edible carrion nest for their larvae by removing any fur or feathers, and rolling the meat into a ball.
evidence: This describes established beetle behavior.

claim: Beetles reduce competition with rival species by smearing the flesh in antimicrobial exudates.
source: The beetles also reduce competition with rival species for the resources on the dead body by smearing the flesh in antimicrobial exudates, consuming eggs laid by rival insects and concealing the body below ground (Chen et al., 2020; Duarte et al., 2018; Scott, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Beetles reduce competition with rival species by consuming eggs laid by rival insects.
source: The beetles also reduce competition with rival species for the resources on the dead body by smearing the flesh in antimicrobial exudates, consuming eggs laid by rival insects and concealing the body below ground (Chen et al., 2020; Duarte et al., 2018; Scott, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Beetles reduce competition with rival species by concealing the body below ground.
source: The beetles also reduce competition with rival species for the resources on the dead body by smearing the flesh in antimicrobial exudates, consuming eggs laid by rival insects and concealing the body below ground (Chen et al., 2020; Duarte et al., 2018; Scott, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Beetle eggs are laid in the surrounding soil and hatch within 3–4 days.
source: During carcass preparation, beetle eggs are laid in the surrounding soil and then hatch within 3–4 days.
evidence: This describes the beetle reproductive timeline.

claim: Beetle larvae crawl to the carcass and feed themselves on the edible nest, where they are also fed and defended by both parents.
source: The larvae crawl to the carcass and feed themselves on the edible nest, where they are also fed and defended by both parents.
evidence: This describes beetle parental care behavior.

claim: Within a week of hatching, beetle larvae disperse away from the carcass to pupate.
source: Within a week of hatching, the larvae disperse away from the scant remains of the carcass to pupate, while adults fly off – often to breed again.
evidence: This describes the beetle life cycle.

claim: Adult burying beetles carry up to 14 species of mites.
source: Adult burying beetles carry up to 14 species of mites, which also breed on carrion and which use the burying beetle as a means of transport between breeding opportunities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about beetle-mite associations.

claim: Mites breed on carrion and use the burying beetle as a means of transport between breeding opportunities.
source: Adult burying beetles carry up to 14 species of mites, which also breed on carrion and which use the burying beetle as a means of transport between breeding opportunities.
evidence: This describes the mite-beetle relationship.

claim: The Poecilochirus carabi species complex is the most salient and common of the mite species carried by burying beetles.
source: The Poecilochirus carabi species complex is the most salient and common of these mite species (e.g. Wilson, 1983; Schwarz et al., 1998), and it is the focus of this study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: P. carabi travels as sexually immature deutonymphs on the burying beetle.
source: P. carabi travels as sexually immature deutonymphs on the burying beetle, and derives no nourishment directly from its host while it is on board (Wilson and Knollenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P. carabi derives no nourishment directly from its host while it is on board.
source: P. carabi travels as sexually immature deutonymphs on the burying beetle, and derives no nourishment directly from its host while it is on board (Wilson and Knollenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Upon arrival at a carcass, the mite deutonymphs alight and moult into adults, which then reproduce.
source: Upon arrival at a carcass, the deutonymphs alight and moult into adults, which then reproduce.
evidence: This describes the mite life cycle.

claim: The next generation of mite deutonymphs is ready to disperse by the time the adult burying beetles cease caring for larvae and leave the breeding event.
source: The next generation of mite deutonymphs is ready to disperse by the time the adult burying beetles cease caring for larvae and leave the breeding event.
evidence: This describes the synchronized timing of beetle and mite life cycles.

claim: Roughly 90% of mite deutonymphs disperse on the departing adult beetles rather than on the burying beetle's larvae.
source: Roughly 90% of deutonymphs disperse on the departing adults rather than on the burying beetle's larvae (Schwarz and Müller, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P. carabi is often described as a phoretic mite because it uses burying beetles to travel between breeding opportunities on carrion.
source: P. carabi is often described as a phoretic mite because it uses burying beetles (Nicrophorus spp.) to travel between breeding opportunities on carrion, and seemingly imposes few costs on its hosts during transportation.
evidence: This describes the classification of the mite-beetle relationship.

claim: P. carabi seemingly imposes few costs on its hosts during transportation.
source: P. carabi is often described as a phoretic mite because it uses burying beetles (Nicrophorus spp.) to travel between breeding opportunities on carrion, and seemingly imposes few costs on its hosts during transportation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the relationship based on existing knowledge.

claim: Phoretic interactions are thought to pave the way for further interactions between host and phoront that have more positive or negative effects on host fitness.
source: Phoretic interactions are thought to pave the way for further interactions between host and phoront that have more positive or negative effects on host fitness.
evidence: This is a general statement about phoretic interactions.

claim: Further interactions between host and phoront are especially likely when interactions endure beyond the transport phase.
source: This is especially likely when interactions between host and phoront endure beyond the transport phase (White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Female Trichogramma parasitoid wasps hitch a relatively cost-free ride to their butterfly hosts' egg-laying site.
source: For example, female Trichogramma parasitoid wasps hitch a relatively cost-free ride to their butterfly hosts' egg-laying site, but upon arrival are easily able to locate butterfly eggs to parasitise (Fatouros and Huigens, 2012).
evidence: This is an example from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Upon arrival at the butterfly egg-laying site, Trichogramma wasps are easily able to locate butterfly eggs to parasitise.
source: For example, female Trichogramma parasitoid wasps hitch a relatively cost-free ride to their butterfly hosts' egg-laying site, but upon arrival are easily able to locate butterfly eggs to parasitise (Fatouros and Huigens, 2012).
evidence: This is an example from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: The phoretic mite Ensliniella parasitica travels on female mason wasps Allodynerus delphinalis.
source: Likewise, the phoretic mite Ensliniella parasitica travels on female mason wasps Allodynerus delphinalis.
evidence: This is an example from previous literature.

claim: Ensliniella parasitica mites are mildly parasitic because they feed on the developing wasp's haemolymph.
source: The mites are mildly parasitic because they feed on the developing wasp's haemolymph (Okabe and Shun'ichi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: If wasp pupae are threatened by parasitoid wasps, Ensliniella parasitica mites protect them from attack, thus switching from parasite to mutualist.
source: However, if the wasp pupae are threatened by parasitoid wasps, the mite protects them from attack, thus switching from parasite to mutualist (Okabe and Shun'ichi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Phoretic interactions are generally under-studied.
source: Nevertheless phoretic interactions are generally under-studied and their capacity to extend into further interactions that influence host fitness remains poorly understood (White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citation.

claim: The capacity of phoretic interactions to extend into further interactions that influence host fitness remains poorly understood.
source: Nevertheless phoretic interactions are generally under-studied and their capacity to extend into further interactions that influence host fitness remains poorly understood (White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citation.

claim: The beetle has a net positive effect on mite fitness.
source: The beetle has a net positive effect on mite fitness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship described.

claim: Without the beetle, the mite would not be able to breed at all.
source: Without the beetle, the mite would not be able to breed at all.
evidence: This is an inference about the dependence of mites on beetles.

claim: Mites have greater reproductive success on beetle-prepared carrion than on other dead meat.
source: Furthermore, mites have greater reproductive success on beetle-prepared carrion than on other dead meat (Sun and Kilner, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In some contexts, the mite reduces burying beetle fitness.
source: However, in some contexts, the mite reduces burying beetle fitness.
evidence: This is a general statement that will be supported by data in the results.

claim: Mite offspring compete with burying beetle larvae for resources on the carcass.
source: Mite offspring compete with burying beetle larvae for resources on the carcass, and can directly predate upon beetle eggs and newly-hatched larvae (Wilson, 1983; Beninger, 1993; De Gasperin and Kilner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mites can directly predate upon beetle eggs and newly-hatched larvae.
source: Mite offspring compete with burying beetle larvae for resources on the carcass, and can directly predate upon beetle eggs and newly-hatched larvae (Wilson, 1983; Beninger, 1993; De Gasperin and Kilner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In some contexts the mites are harmful for the burying beetle.
source: Thus, in some contexts the mites are harmful for the burying beetle.
evidence: This is an inference from the competition and predation described.

claim: In other contexts, the mite can potentially become a protective mutualist by defending burying beetle reproductive success when it is threatened by an enemy species.
source: In other contexts, though, the mite can potentially become a protective mutualist by defending burying beetle reproductive success when it is threatened by an enemy species (Wilson, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Blowflies are a particular competitive threat for burying beetles.
source: Blowflies (Calliphoridae) are a particular competitive threat for burying beetles (Scott, 1994; Sun et al., 2014) because they can locate the newly dead more rapidly than burying beetles (within a few hours: Shelomi et al., 2012); personal observations) and start to lay eggs within minutes of arriving on the dead body (Bornemissza, 1957; Matuszewski et al., 2010; Payne, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blowflies can locate the newly dead more rapidly than burying beetles (within a few hours).
source: Blowflies (Calliphoridae) are a particular competitive threat for burying beetles (Scott, 1994; Sun et al., 2014) because they can locate the newly dead more rapidly than burying beetles (within a few hours: Shelomi et al., 2012); personal observations) and start to lay eggs within minutes of arriving on the dead body (Bornemissza, 1957; Matuszewski et al., 2010; Payne, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation and personal observations.

claim: Blowflies start to lay eggs within minutes of arriving on the dead body.
source: Blowflies (Calliphoridae) are a particular competitive threat for burying beetles (Scott, 1994; Sun et al., 2014) because they can locate the newly dead more rapidly than burying beetles (within a few hours: Shelomi et al., 2012); personal observations) and start to lay eggs within minutes of arriving on the dead body (Bornemissza, 1957; Matuszewski et al., 2010; Payne, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mites can potentially prevent burying beetles from losing fitness to rival blowflies by eating blowfly eggs.
source: Mites can potentially prevent burying beetles from losing fitness to rival blowflies by eating blowfly eggs (Springett, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: As an indirect effect of the mites' predatory actions, the net fitness outcome of the mite-beetle interaction becomes positive-positive.
source: As an indirect effect of the mites' predatory actions, the net fitness outcome of the mite-beetle interaction becomes positive-positive.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of mite predation on blowflies.

claim: Since the mite is only able to feed upon blowflies because it was transported to the carrion by the burying beetle, the mite becomes a mutualist.
source: Since the mite is only able to feed upon blowflies because it was transported to the carrion by the burying beetle, the mite becomes a mutualist.
evidence: This is an inference about the mutualistic nature of the relationship.

claim: At higher temperatures blowflies pose a greater threat to burying beetle and mite fitness.
source: Previous work has shown that at higher temperatures blowflies pose a greater threat to burying beetle and mite fitness.
evidence: This is stated as previous work.

claim: Blowflies are more abundant on carrion at higher temperatures.
source: Blowflies are more abundant on carrion at higher temperatures, develop more rapidly and have higher reproductive success (Sun et al., 2014; Wall et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blowflies develop more rapidly at higher temperatures.
source: Blowflies are more abundant on carrion at higher temperatures, develop more rapidly and have higher reproductive success (Sun et al., 2014; Wall et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blowflies have higher reproductive success at higher temperatures.
source: Blowflies are more abundant on carrion at higher temperatures, develop more rapidly and have higher reproductive success (Sun et al., 2014; Wall et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: High densities of mites might be more effective at protecting from blowflies under high temperature conditions.
source: High densities of mites might be more effective at protecting from blowflies under these conditions (Okabe and Shun'ichi, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous work, indicated by 'might be'.

claim: High densities of phoretic mites and phoretic nematodes are known to reduce the number and quality of burying beetle larvae produced.
source: Yet high densities of phoretic mites and phoretic nematodes are also known to reduce the number and quality of burying beetle larvae produced, potentially making mites more harmful (De Gasperin and Kilner, 2016; Wang and Rozen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is unclear how temperature, mite density, and the presence of blowflies interact to determine whether interactions between mites and their burying beetles are harmful to beetles or more mutualistic.
source: Therefore it is unclear how these three factors (temperature, mite density, and the presence of blowflies) interact to determine whether interactions between mites and their burying beetles are harmful to beetles or more mutualistic.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Burying beetle reproductive success peaked at intermediate temperatures, and dipped at lower and higher temperatures.
source: Whereas burying beetle reproductive success peaked at intermediate temperatures, and dipped at lower and higher temperatures (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1a), blowflies had greatest reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures and much less success at intermediate temperatures (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and statistical analysis.

claim: Blowflies had greatest reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures and much less success at intermediate temperatures.
source: Whereas burying beetle reproductive success peaked at intermediate temperatures, and dipped at lower and higher temperatures (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1a), blowflies had greatest reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures and much less success at intermediate temperatures (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and statistical analysis.

claim: When 10 mites were added, there was little effect on the overall reproductive success of beetles.
source: When we added 10 mites, there was little effect on the overall reproductive success of beetles (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1a), though mites significantly reduced the reproductive success of the blowflies at lower and higher temperature ranges (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: When 10 mites were added, mites significantly reduced the reproductive success of the blowflies at lower and higher temperature ranges.
source: When we added 10 mites, there was little effect on the overall reproductive success of beetles (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1a), though mites significantly reduced the reproductive success of the blowflies at lower and higher temperature ranges (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: When 20 mites were added, mites were especially effective at promoting beetle reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures.
source: When we added 20 mites, however, mites were especially effective at promoting beetle reproductive success at these same lower and higher temperatures (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis.

claim: When 20 mites were added, they caused a corresponding decline in the success of blowflies breeding at lower and higher temperatures.
source: Once again, they caused a corresponding decline in the success of blowflies breeding at lower and higher temperatures (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and statistical analysis.

claim: Variation in mite reproductive success could not be explained by temperature.
source: Turning to the mites' perspective, we found that variation in their reproductive success could not be explained by temperature (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Mites act as protective mutualists for burying beetles against blowflies in natural breeding conditions.
source: From these initial results, we conclude that mites act as protective mutualists for burying beetles against blowflies in natural breeding conditions, matching results obtained previously for a different burying beetle species (Wilson, 1983), and that their effects are contingent on mite density per breeding event.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the field experiment data and supported by citation.

claim: The effects of mites as protective mutualists are contingent on mite density per breeding event.
source: From these initial results, we conclude that mites act as protective mutualists for burying beetles against blowflies in natural breeding conditions, matching results obtained previously for a different burying beetle species (Wilson, 1983), and that their effects are contingent on mite density per breeding event.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the field experiment data.

claim: Mites promote burying beetle reproductive success specifically at lower and higher temperatures.
source: Our results extend the findings of previous work by showing that mites promote burying beetle reproductive success specifically at lower and higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the field experiment data.

claim: Blowflies reduced burying beetle reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures.
source: We found that blowflies reduced burying beetle reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures (interaction blowfly treatment x temperature treatment, χ2 = 25.85, d.f. = 2, p<0.001), and that blowflies caused greater reduction at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures (post-hoc comparison high v. low, z = −2.47, p=0.036).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of laboratory experiment data.

claim: Blowflies caused greater reduction in beetle reproductive success at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures.
source: We found that blowflies reduced burying beetle reproductive success at lower and higher temperatures (interaction blowfly treatment x temperature treatment, χ2 = 25.85, d.f. = 2, p<0.001), and that blowflies caused greater reduction at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures (post-hoc comparison high v. low, z = −2.47, p=0.036).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of laboratory experiment data.

claim: Burying beetles substantially reduced blowfly reproductive success but the effect was temperature-dependent.
source: We found that burying beetles substantially reduced blowfly reproductive success but that the effect was temperature-dependent (interaction beetle x temperature treatments: χ2 = 38.32, d.f. = 2, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing Laboratory Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Blowfly reproductive success was most strongly reduced by beetles at intermediate temperatures.
source: Blowfly reproductive success was most strongly reduced by beetles at intermediate temperatures (z = 10.59, p<0.001), with a less pronounced decrease at lower temperatures (z = 9.40, p<0.001), and the least change of all at higher temperatures (z = 7.04, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Blowflies reduced mite reproductive success.
source: Further analyses of Laboratory Experiment 1 revealed that blowflies reduced mite reproductive success (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1b) and that the extent of mite fitness loss was modulated by temperature (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and statistical analysis.

claim: The extent of mite fitness loss due to blowflies was modulated by temperature.
source: Further analyses of Laboratory Experiment 1 revealed that blowflies reduced mite reproductive success (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1b) and that the extent of mite fitness loss was modulated by temperature (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Blowflies reduced mite reproductive success at mid and higher temperatures.
source: We found that blowflies reduced mite reproductive success at mid and higher temperatures (mid temperatures: post-hoc comparison without blowflies v. with blowflies, z = 2.24, p=0.025; higher temperatures: post-hoc comparison without blowflies v. with blowflies, z = 3.29, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Blowflies had no effect on mite reproductive success at lower temperatures.
source: However, blowflies had no effect on mite reproductive success at lower temperatures (post-hoc comparison without blowflies v. with blowflies, z = 0.30, p=0.766).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Temperature modulates the negative effects of the blowfly on both burying beetle and mite fitness.
source: Temperature thus modulates the negative effects of the blowfly on both burying beetle and mite fitness (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the laboratory experiment data.

claim: Adding mites generally reduced burying beetle reproductive success, though to different degrees at different mite densities.
source: Adding mites generally reduced burying beetle reproductive success, though to different degrees at different mite densities (Figure 2A-C; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C and statistical analysis.

claim: Across all temperatures, mites had no effect on beetle reproductive success in groups of 10.
source: Across all temperatures, mites had no effect on beetle reproductive success in groups of 10 (post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = 1.49, p=0.298).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Adding 20 mites significantly reduced beetle reproductive success.
source: However, adding 20 mites significantly reduced beetle reproductive success (post-hoc comparison 0 v. 20 mites, z = 3.20, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Mites have mildly negative effects on burying beetle fitness.
source: Therefore, mites have mildly negative effects on burying beetle fitness, as has been reported before in previous work on N. vespilloides (Beninger, 1993; De Gasperin and Kilner, 2015; Nehring et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019) and other Nicrophorus species (Wilson and Knollenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The loss in beetle reproductive success caused by mites at high temperatures was much less than that induced by blowflies.
source: Nevertheless, the loss in beetle reproductive success caused by mites at high temperatures was much less than that induced by blowflies (post-hoc comparison 0 mites, with blowflies v. 10 mites, without blowflies, z = −3.61, p=0.002; post-hoc comparison 0 mites, with blowflies v. 20 mites, without blowflies, z = −2.85, p=0.023).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The presence of blowflies caused mites to switch to becoming more mutualistic.
source: We found that the presence of blowflies caused mites to switch to becoming more mutualistic.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the laboratory experiment data.

claim: The extent of mutualism was dependent both on temperature and mite density.
source: Furthermore, the extent of mutualism was dependent both on temperature and mite density, matching our findings in the field.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the laboratory experiment data.

claim: At lower temperatures, neither density of mites affected beetle reproductive success when blowflies were present.
source: At lower temperatures, neither density of mites affected beetle reproductive success when blowflies were present (post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = −0.77, p=0.720; Figure 2E; post-hoc comparison 0 v. 20 mites, z = −0.60, p=0.822; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: At higher temperatures, 10 mites had no effect on burying beetle reproductive success.
source: At higher temperatures, 10 mites had no effect on burying beetle reproductive success either (post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = −1.03, p=0.560; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When 20 mites were added to the breeding event, they increased beetle reproductive success but only at higher temperatures.
source: However, when 20 mites were added to the breeding event, they increased beetle reproductive success but only at higher temperatures (post-hoc comparison 0 v. 20 mites, z = −3.04, p=0.007; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The increase in beetle reproductive success was matched by a corresponding mite-induced decline in blowfly reproductive success.
source: The increase in beetle reproductive success was matched by a corresponding mite-induced decline in blowfly reproductive success (Figure 3), with the pattern of decline again matching the results of our field experiment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When there were no mites present, blowflies breeding alongside burying beetles had much greater reproductive success at higher temperatures and lower temperatures than at intermediate temperatures.
source: When there were no mites present, blowflies breeding alongside burying beetles had much greater reproductive success at higher temperatures and lower temperatures than at intermediate temperatures (post-hoc comparison high v. mid temperature, z = 5.61, p<0.001; post-hoc comparison low v. mid temperature, z = 3.21, p=0.004; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Burying beetles can manage singlehandedly to defend their reproductive success against blowflies at intermediate temperatures.
source: In summary, the field and lab experimental results each suggest that burying beetles can manage singlehandedly to defend their reproductive success against blowflies at intermediate temperatures, but that they struggle to produce as many larvae at higher and lower temperatures (Figure 1B, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from field and lab experiments.

claim: Burying beetles struggle to produce as many larvae at higher and lower temperatures.
source: In summary, the field and lab experimental results each suggest that burying beetles can manage singlehandedly to defend their reproductive success against blowflies at intermediate temperatures, but that they struggle to produce as many larvae at higher and lower temperatures (Figure 1B, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from field and lab experiments.

claim: Adding 10 mites did not cause a significant reduction in the number of blowfly larvae produced at lower and higher temperatures.
source: Although adding 10 mites did not cause a significant reduction in the number of blowfly larvae produced (lower temperatures: post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = 1.76, p=0.183; higher temperatures: post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = −0.65, p=0.792; Figure 3B), adding 20 mites to the breeding event caused blowflies to perform badly at all temperatures (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Adding 20 mites to the breeding event caused blowflies to perform badly at all temperatures.
source: Although adding 10 mites did not cause a significant reduction in the number of blowfly larvae produced (lower temperatures: post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = 1.76, p=0.183; higher temperatures: post-hoc comparison 0 v. 10 mites, z = −0.65, p=0.792; Figure 3B), adding 20 mites to the breeding event caused blowflies to perform badly at all temperatures (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Burying beetles and mites wander all over the carrion nest, especially during carcass preparation before the burying beetle larvae hatch.
source: Both species wander all over the carrion nest, especially during carcass preparation before the burying beetle larvae hatch (Smiseth et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Burying beetles and mites graze on the surface of the carrion as they go.
source: They graze on the surface of the carrion as they go, and have been observed to consume blowflies when they are eggs or newly hatched 1st instar blowfly larvae (Wilson, 1983; Wilson and Knollenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Burying beetles and mites have been observed to consume blowflies when they are eggs or newly hatched 1st instar blowfly larvae.
source: They graze on the surface of the carrion as they go, and have been observed to consume blowflies when they are eggs or newly hatched 1st instar blowfly larvae (Wilson, 1983; Wilson and Knollenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The likelihood that blowfly eggs will be eaten depends partly on the duration of vulnerable early life stages during blowfly development.
source: The likelihood that blowfly eggs will be eaten therefore depends partly on the duration of these vulnerable early life stages during blowfly development, and partly on the extent to which beetles and mites prey upon blowflies.
evidence: This is an inference about factors affecting predation on blowflies.

claim: The likelihood that blowfly eggs will be eaten depends partly on the extent to which beetles and mites prey upon blowflies.
source: The likelihood that blowfly eggs will be eaten therefore depends partly on the duration of these vulnerable early life stages during blowfly development, and partly on the extent to which beetles and mites prey upon blowflies.
evidence: This is an inference about factors affecting predation on blowflies.

claim: Temperature could not explain any variation in blowfly reproductive success.
source: We found that temperature could not explain any variation in either blowfly reproductive success (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1c), or the extent to which blowfly larvae consumed the carcass (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Temperature could not explain variation in the extent to which blowfly larvae consumed the carcass.
source: We found that temperature could not explain any variation in either blowfly reproductive success (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1c), or the extent to which blowfly larvae consumed the carcass (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blowfly development was greatly accelerated at higher temperatures.
source: However, blowfly development was greatly accelerated at higher temperatures (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 1c), with blowflies spending significantly less time as eggs and 1st instar larvae at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures (eggs: t = −3.76, p<0.001; 1st: t = −4.89, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blowflies spent significantly less time as eggs at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures.
source: However, blowfly development was greatly accelerated at higher temperatures (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 1c), with blowflies spending significantly less time as eggs and 1st instar larvae at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures (eggs: t = −3.76, p<0.001; 1st: t = −4.89, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blowflies spent significantly less time as 1st instar larvae at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures.
source: However, blowfly development was greatly accelerated at higher temperatures (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 1c), with blowflies spending significantly less time as eggs and 1st instar larvae at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures (eggs: t = −3.76, p<0.001; 1st: t = −4.89, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Carcass preparation by beetles reduced the number of blowfly larvae produced and its effectiveness was sensitive to temperature.
source: When we compared the number of blowfly larvae produced in Laboratory Experiment 2, when beetles were able to prepare a carcass, and Laboratory Experiment 3, when beetles were absent, we found that carcass preparation by beetles reduced the number of blowfly larvae produced and but that its effectiveness was sensitive to temperature (interaction carcass preparation x temperature treatments: χ2 = 19.67, d.f. = 2, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing Laboratory Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: Blowflies showed the greatest loss in fitness at intermediate temperatures due to beetle carcass preparation.
source: Blowflies showed the greatest loss in fitness at intermediate temperatures (z = 9.84, p<0.001) with a less marked reduction in fitness at lower (z = 5.16, p<0.001) and higher temperatures (z = 6.25, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The effectiveness of carcass preparation by beetles varied with temperature.
source: We found that the effectiveness of carcass preparation by beetles varied with temperature (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Beetles converted a dead body into a rounder nest for their larvae at both higher and mid temperatures than at lower temperatures.
source: Specifically, beetles converted a dead body into a rounder nest for their larvae at both higher and mid temperatures than at lower temperatures (post-hoc comparison high v. low, z = 4.68, p<0.001; post-hoc comparison low v. mid, z = −4.83, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The rounder the prepared carcass was, the fewer the blowfly larvae that survived.
source: The rounder the prepared carcass was, the fewer the blowfly larvae that survived (χ2 = 13.78, d.f. = 1, p<0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The combined effects of temperature on both carcass preparation by beetles and blowfly development explain why blowflies are able to produce more larvae at higher and lower temperatures than at mid temperatures.
source: The combined effects of temperature on both carcass preparation by beetles and blowfly development, explain why blowflies are able to produce more larvae at higher and lower temperatures than at mid temperatures - and therefore why they pose more of a threat to burying beetle and mite fitness at these temperatures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Blowflies pose more of a threat to burying beetle and mite fitness at higher and lower temperatures.
source: The combined effects of temperature on both carcass preparation by beetles and blowfly development, explain why blowflies are able to produce more larvae at higher and lower temperatures than at mid temperatures - and therefore why they pose more of a threat to burying beetle and mite fitness at these temperatures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Burying beetles can singlehandedly defend themselves against blowflies at intermediate temperatures through their activities during carcass preparation.
source: Burying beetles can singlehandedly defend themselves against blowflies at intermediate temperatures through their activities during carcass preparation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: At higher temperatures, blowflies develop sufficiently rapidly that they can evade beetle defences.
source: At higher temperatures, blowflies develop sufficiently rapidly that they can evade these beetle defences.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: At lower temperatures, burying beetles are less able to defend themselves against blowflies during carcass preparation.
source: At lower temperatures, burying beetles are less able to defend themselves against blowflies during carcass preparation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The interaction between burying beetles and their P. carabi mites depends on whether blowflies are present.
source: However, the interaction between burying beetles and their P. carabi mites depends on whether blowflies are present too - because predation by mites on blowfly eggs then indirectly enhances burying beetle reproductive success.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Predation by mites on blowfly eggs indirectly enhances burying beetle reproductive success.
source: However, the interaction between burying beetles and their P. carabi mites depends on whether blowflies are present too - because predation by mites on blowfly eggs then indirectly enhances burying beetle reproductive success.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The extent of mutualism varies with increasing temperature stress.
source: The extent of mutualism also varies with increasing temperature stress, and with increasing mite density.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The extent of mutualism varies with increasing mite density.
source: The extent of mutualism also varies with increasing temperature stress, and with increasing mite density.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Temperature, mite density, and blowfly presence cause a corresponding change in the net fitness outcome for burying beetles.
source: All three factors cause a corresponding change in the net fitness outcome for burying beetles and this determines whether the mite harms burying beetle fitness or is more mutualistic (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Mites were antagonistic to beetles at all temperatures in the absence of blowflies.
source: Consistent with previous work on other burying beetle species (Wilson, 1983), we found that mites were antagonistic to beetles at all temperatures in the absence of blowflies (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: A similar decrease in the extent of mutualism has been detected in other protective mutualisms when the third-party enemy species is absent or removed.
source: A similar decrease in the extent of mutualism has been detected in other protective mutualisms when the third-party enemy species is absent or removed (Hopkins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: It is common for the host to reduce the rewards it offers its protective mutualist when the enemy is absent.
source: Then, it is common for the host to reduce the rewards it offers its protective mutualist (Palmer et al., 2015; Palmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is unclear whether burying beetles reduce the rewards they offer to mites when blowflies are absent.
source: It is unclear whether this happens in burying beetles too.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: The main service that beetles offer to mites is transport to carrion.
source: However, the main service that beetles offer to mites is transport to carrion.
evidence: This is based on the established relationship between beetles and mites.

claim: It is hard to see how beetles could accurately modulate the transport service they offer to mites in relation to the prevalence of blowflies.
source: Either way, since the prevalence of blowflies is likely to vary locally from one breeding attempt to the next, it is hard to see how beetles could accurately modulate the transport service they offer to mites in relation to the prevalence of blowflies.
evidence: This is speculation about the difficulty of modulating the mutualism.

claim: Some of the other mite species carried by burying beetles in nature, or the phoretic nematodes, might modulate the harm inflicted by P. carabi on its burying beetle host.
source: An alternative possibility is that some of the other mite species carried by burying beetles in nature (which we excluded from our experiments), or the phoretic nematodes that are also present upon the beetle (Wang and Rozen, 2019) modulate the harm inflicted by P. carabi on its burying beetle host.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms, with citation.

claim: Whether other mite species or nematodes modulate the harm inflicted by P. carabi remains to be determined in future work.
source: Whether this actually happens, however, remains to be determined in future work.
evidence: This identifies a question for future research.

claim: Previous studies have emphasised the significance of the abiotic environment in shifting the outcome of species interactions.
source: Previous studies have emphasised the significance of the abiotic environment in shifting the outcome of species interactions (Chamberlain et al., 2014; Gorter et al., 2016; Hoeksema and Bruna, 2015; Hopkins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Protective mutualisms sometimes break down at higher temperatures because the protecting partner is more vulnerable to heat stress when temperatures rise.
source: Protective mutualisms sometimes break down at higher temperatures because the protecting partner is more vulnerable to heat stress when temperatures rise (Barton and Ives, 2014; Doremus and Oliver, 2017; Fitzpatrick et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There was no evidence that mites were more vulnerable to higher temperatures, whether in field or laboratory conditions.
source: However, we found no evidence that mites were more vulnerable to higher temperatures, whether in field or laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data.

claim: The main driver of change in the protective mutualism came from the response of enemy blowflies, and the behaviour of the burying beetles themselves, to variation in temperature.
source: Instead, the main driver of change in the protective mutualism came from the response of enemy blowflies, and the behaviour of the burying beetles themselves, to variation in temperature (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Similar effects might be found in other protective mutualisms where enemy species are more likely to thrive at high temperatures, providing that both partners can tolerate some thermal stress.
source: We suggest that similar effects might be found in other protective mutualisms where enemy species are more likely to thrive at high temperatures, providing that both partners can tolerate some thermal stress.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Predicting how populations might respond to more variable temperatures involves understanding its interactions within the natural ecological community as well as some knowledge of the intrinsic variation in the thermal tolerance of the mutualistic partner.
source: Predicting how populations might respond to more variable temperatures thus involves understanding its interactions within the natural ecological community as well as some knowledge of the intrinsic variation in the thermal tolerance of the mutualistic partner (Early and Keith, 2019).
evidence: This is a general conclusion with citation.

claim: The mites' capacity to defend burying beetles against competition from blowflies was both temperature-dependent and density-dependent.
source: The mites' capacity to defend burying beetles against competition from blowflies was both temperature-dependent and density-dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: In the field and in the lab, blowflies posed a greater threat to burying beetle fitness at higher temperatures and then it took a high density of mites to neutralize this danger.
source: In the field and in the lab, blowflies posed a greater threat to burying beetle fitness at higher temperatures and then it took a high density of mites to neutralize this danger.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Increased mite density has been found to influence the effectiveness of defences against enemy species in other protective mutualisms as well.
source: Increased mite density has been found to influence the effectiveness of defences against enemy species in other protective mutualisms as well (e.g. Okabe and Shun'ichi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The experiments captured the likely variation in mite density at natural breeding events.
source: Our experiments captured the likely variation in mite density at natural breeding events.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: There is no evidence to suggest that beetles can regulate the density of mites they carry in anticipation of the threats they face to their reproductive success.
source: However, we have no evidence to suggest that beetles can regulate the density of mites they carry in anticipation of the threats they face to their reproductive success (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The expression of a protective mutualism between burying beetles and their P. carabi mites is context-dependent and depends on a complex interplay of biotic and abiotic factors.
source: In conclusion, we have shown how the expression of a protective mutualism between burying beetles and their P. carabi mites is context-dependent and depends on a complex interplay of biotic and abiotic factors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Short-term variation in the expression of this protective mutualism may influence the capacity of its host burying beetle to persist in adverse environments.
source: In common with other facultatively expressed mutualisms (Afkhami et al., 2014; Johnson, 2015; Peay, 2016), short-term variation in the expression of this protective mutualism may influence the capacity of its host burying beetle to persist in adverse environments.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications, with citations.

claim: Fieldwork was carried out at Madingley Woods in Cambridgeshire UK, an ancient woodland of mixed deciduous trees.
source: Fieldwork was carried out at Madingley Woods in Cambridgeshire UK, an ancient woodland (Goldberg et al., 2007) of mixed deciduous trees near the Sub-Department of Animal Behaviour, University of Cambridge, (Latitude: 52.22730°; Longitude: 0.04442°).
evidence: This describes the study site, with citation.

claim: The mean time for beetles to discover baited traps was 3.42 ± 0.77 days.
source: The mean ± S.E.M. time to discovery was 3.42 ± 0.77 days.
evidence: This is data from the field observations.

claim: Field-caught burying beetles naturally carried a mean of 10.82 ± 0.45 mites.
source: Field-caught burying beetles naturally carried a mean ± S.E.M. of 10.82 ± 0.45 mites (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 from Sun et al., 2019 for frequency distribution of mite density), while 70% of them carried 1–20 mites (n = 1369 beetles).
evidence: This is data from field observations.

claim: 70% of field-caught beetles carried 1–20 mites.
source: Field-caught burying beetles naturally carried a mean ± S.E.M. of 10.82 ± 0.45 mites (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 from Sun et al., 2019 for frequency distribution of mite density), while 70% of them carried 1–20 mites (n = 1369 beetles).
evidence: This is data from field observations.

claim: A temperature-enhanced threat from blowflies causes mites to become protective mutualists of their burying beetle hosts.
source: Our overall conclusion is that a temperature-enhanced threat from blowflies causes mites to become protective mutualists of their burying beetle hosts.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion of the study, as stated in Figure 5 caption.
